newsitem.title: USA: U.S. patent lawsuits spur interest in insurance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. patent lawsuits spur interest in insurance.

text.p: A growing number of patent infringement lawsuits, like the one Digital Equipment Corp filed against Intel Corp this week, are spurring interest in insurance products to protect both the plaintiff and the defendant.
However, the amount of coverage available is still quite limited, with just a handful of insurers participating in the market.
But, because it is a "growth area of the legal system, it's bound to become a bigger insurance market at some point," one insurance industry source said.

Patent infringement actions have increased steadily in recent years, with the number of patent cases up 6.8 percent to 1,840 in 1996 and up nearly 25 percent over 1992, according to the 1996 Annual Report of the Director of the Administrative Office of the United States Courts.
Digital earlier this week claimed Intel infringed on 10 of its patents to make Pentium computer chips.
Digital is seeking to force Intel to stop using its technology and wants triple monetary damages, according to the lawsuit.
Intel said it does not believe its Pentium chips infringe on Digital's patents and will vigorously defend itself.
However, Intel said it does not carry patent infringement liability insurance because of the limited market and low coverage limits. Digital declined immediate comment on its insurance coverage.

Companies seeking protection against patent infringement lawsuits can obtain coverage from American International Group Inc, which offers a policy covering up to $15 million in liability and defense costs for defendants in patent cases.

The policy, which was first introduced in 1994, insures companies against claims of U.S. patent infringement in the manufacture, sale, use, distribution and advertisement of covered products and processes, AIG said.
Patent infringement claims also can be covered under commercial general liability policies, said David Einhorn, a New York partner and intellectual property specialist at Anderson Kill & Olick.
Meanwhile, patent owners can buy insurance to help cover the legal costs associated with enforcing their patents from Lloyd's of London and Homestead Insurance Co.

"The true value of the patent can only be realized if the patent owner has got the wherewithal to enforce it if someone decides to infringe on it," said Donald Fancher, director of litigation services for Deloitte & Touche LLP in Houston.

Legal costs to defend a patent average about $1.2 million and that can be a barrier preventing some companies from protecting their patents, said Joby Hughes, president of Litigation Risk Management Inc in Houston, Texas and creator of the patent protection insurance underwritten by Lloyds.
He said he believes demand for such insurance will rise as more companies depend on their intellectual property and patents to differentiate themselves from their competitors.
The Lloyd's and Litigation Risk policy was launched in March and offers $1 million in coverage, with a 20 percent co-pay. Higher limits are available.
Hughes said he has already received about 500 inquiries about the product since March and dozens of phone calls this week following news of Digital's lawsuit against Intel.
Lloyd's and Litigation Risk also offer a policy to help defendants pay their legal costs, said Fancher, who works with Litigation Risk to analyze the economic value of the property to be insured.
But unlike the American International policy, the Lloyd's policy does not cover liability costs, Fancher said.
Homestead also underwrites policies up to $500,000 in coverage for legal expenses through its managing general agent, Intellectual Property Insurance Services Corp.
